title: The Hidden Cost of Higher Mortgage Rates
text:
On September 16, 2026, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) raised its federal-funds target range by 25 basis points to 3.75%–4.00%. Short-term benchmark rates adjusted immediately, but homebuyers do not borrow overnight: they usually finance a purchase for 15 or 30 years. This post asks a practical question:
The answer matters because buyers often shop by listing price when the binding constraint is actually monthly cash flow. I combine scraped policy, mortgage, and housing-market information with standard mortgage mathematics to translate an observed weekly rate difference into household-level dollar amounts.

title: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors: The Hidden Engines of Linear Dynamics
text:
Most relationships that economists put on a computer are, at their core, linear: regressions, vector autoregressions (VARs), Markov transition matrices, state-space models, and even the local approximations used to solve dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) models. Every one of these tools repeatedly multiplies vectors by matrices.
A natural question follows:

When we multiply by the same matrix over and over, what happens in the long run — and why?

The complete answer is given by two objects that live inside the matrix itself: its eigenvalues and eigenvectors. This post explains what they are, how to compute them by hand and in R, and why they do so much of the heavy lifting in economics — from the long-run unemployment rate to whether an estimated macro model is even stable.

title: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors: The Hidden Engines of Linear Dynamics
section: 2.1 Finding them: the characteristic equation
text:
2.1 Finding them: the characteristic equation
Moving \(\lambda\mathbf{v}\) to the left and inserting the identity matrix \(\mathbf{I}\) gives
\[
(\mathbf{A} - \lambda\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}.
\]
A non-zero solution \(\mathbf{v}\) exists exactly when the matrix \((\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})\) is singular, i.e. its determinant is zero:
\[
\det(\mathbf{A} - \lambda\mathbf{I}) = 0.
\]
This is the characteristic equation. It produces a polynomial in \(\lambda\) whose \(n\) roots are the eigenvalues; substituting each root back into \((\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}\) gives the eigenvectors.

title: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors: The Hidden Engines of Linear Dynamics
section: 2.2 A worked 2 × 2 example
text:
2.2 A worked 2 × 2 example
Take the symmetric matrix
\[
\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
The characteristic equation is
\[
\det\begin{pmatrix} 2-\lambda & 1 \\ 1 & 2-\lambda \end{pmatrix}
= (2-\lambda)^2 - 1
= \lambda^2 - 4\lambda + 3
= (\lambda - 1)(\lambda - 3) = 0,
\]
so the eigenvalues are \(\lambda_1 = 3\) and \(\lambda_2 = 1\). The eigenvectors (defined only up to scale, so conventionally normalized to unit length) are
\[
\lambda_1 = 3: \quad \mathbf{v}_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt 2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\lambda_2 = 1: \quad \mathbf{v}_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt 2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Quick check: along the \(45^\circ\) direction, \(\mathbf{A}(1,1)' = (3,3)' = 3(1,1)'\), so the matrix stretches that direction threefold; along \((1,-1)'\) it leaves the vector exactly unchanged.

title: The Hidden Cost of a Rate Hike
section: The first pass-through was immediate
text:
The first pass-through was immediate
The H.15 table shows the effective federal-funds rate moving from 3.63% on September 16 to 3.88% on September 17. The bank prime rate simultaneously moved from 6.75% to 7.00%. Freddie Mac’s national average 30-year fixed mortgage rate rose from 6.76% on September 10 to 6.95% on September 17—a 19-basis-point weekly increase. PMMS reflects thousands of conforming purchase-loan applications, so it is more informative than a single advertised quote.


Show the reproducible R code
p1 <- pmms |>
  filter(date >= ymd("2026-01-01"), date <= ymd("2026-09-17")) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, mortgage_30y)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9, color = "#24496e") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = ymd("2026-09-16"), linetype = "dashed", color = "#b24c3d") +
  geom_point(
    data = analysis_rates,
    size = 3,
    color = "#b24c3d"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 0.1)) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%b") +
  labs(
    title = "The 30-year mortgage rate climbed to 6.95%",
    subtitle = "Weekly national average, 2026 through September 17",
    x = NULL,
    y = "30-year fixed mortgage rate"
  )

p1
ggsave(here("figures", "mortgage-rate-trend.png"), p1, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)








Figure 1: Mortgage rates were already repricing before the September FOMC meeting. The highlighted points define the before-and-after affordability comparison. Source: Freddie Mac PMMS; author’s calculations.

title: The Hidden Cost of a Rate Hike
section: Translating rates into a household budget
text:
Translating rates into a household budget
For principal \(L\), monthly rate \(r\), and \(N=360\) payments, monthly principal and interest are
\[
M=L\frac{r(1+r)^N}{(1+r)^N-1}.
\]
Using the Census Bureau’s July 2026 median new-home price of $393,800 and a 20% down payment, the observed weekly mortgage-rate increase raises monthly principal and interest from $2,045 to $2,085. That is $480 more per year, before property tax, insurance, maintenance, or HOA fees.


Show the reproducible R code
payment_grid <- crossing(
  mortgage_rate = seq(0.04, 0.08, by = 0.0005),
  loan = c(300000, 400000, 500000)
) |>
  mutate(monthly_payment = mortgage_payment(loan, mortgage_rate))

p2 <- ggplot(payment_grid, aes(mortgage_rate, monthly_payment, color = factor(loan))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(rate_before, rate_after), linetype = c("dotted", "dashed")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 0.1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = dollar_format()) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("#3f7d5c", "#c17b31", "#8d4773"),
    labels = dollar(c(300000, 400000, 500000))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Small rate changes compound over 360 payments",
    subtitle = "Monthly principal and interest by loan size",
    x = "Mortgage rate",
    y = "Monthly payment",
    color = "Loan amount"
  )

p2
ggsave(here("figures", "payment-curves.png"), p2, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)








Figure 2: A higher rate raises the payment on the same loan. Calculations assume a 30-year fixed mortgage and show principal and interest only.





The reverse calculation is more useful for buyers. Holding the payment budget fixed,
\[
L_{max}=M\frac{1-(1+r)^{-N}}{r},
\]
so a higher rate reduces the loan a household can support.


Show the reproducible R code
budget_results <- crossing(
  monthly_budget = c(2000, 2500, 3000),
  period = factor(c("Before: 6.76%", "After: 6.95%"), levels = c("Before: 6.76%", "After: 6.95%"))
) |>
  mutate(
    rate = if_else(period == "Before: 6.76%", rate_before, rate_after),
    max_home_price = max_loan(monthly_budget, rate) / 0.80
  )

p3 <- ggplot(budget_results, aes(factor(monthly_budget), max_home_price, fill = period)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = dollar(max_home_price, accuracy = 1000)),
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.75),
    vjust = -0.35,
    size = 3.6
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = dollar_format(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#7396b8", "#c65d45")) +
  labs(
    title = "The rate increase reduced purchasing power",
    subtitle = "Maximum home price supported by a fixed monthly budget",
    x = "Monthly principal-and-interest budget",
    y = "Maximum home price",
    fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

p3
ggsave(here("figures", "buying-power.png"), p3, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)








Figure 3: At a fixed monthly budget, a higher mortgage rate reduces the maximum affordable home price. Assumptions: 30-year term, 20% down, principal and interest only.

title: The Hidden Cost of a Rate Hike
section: Takeaway: budget first, price second
text:
Takeaway: budget first, price second
The latest hike matters to buyers because higher financing costs reduce purchasing power even if house prices do not change. Yet the 19-basis-point weekly mortgage move is not a causal estimate of the Fed announcement: markets anticipated the meeting, and long-term rates and mortgage spreads moved at the same time.
The actionable response is therefore not to predict the next FOMC decision. Buyers should set a payment ceiling first, include taxes and insurance, and stress-test the budget at rates 50–100 basis points above today’s quote. Refinancing may become possible later, but it should not be required for the purchase to remain affordable. The central lesson is simple: the relevant price of a house is not its listing price alone; it is the cash-flow commitment created jointly by the price and the financing rate.

section: Research design: from websites to a decision
text:
Research design: from websites to a decision
The analysis follows a transparent pipeline:

Collect: scrape four public webpages with rvest and cache one dated HTML copy of each page.
Clean: convert table headings into dates, percentage strings into decimals, and price text into a numeric dollar value.
Validate: require the policy and mortgage observations used in the comparison to be present and nonmissing.
Calculate: apply the fixed-rate mortgage annuity formula under explicit assumptions.
Decide: convert the estimates into budget and stress-testing recommendations for prospective buyers.


Sources and ethical access








Source
Scraped information
Role in the analysis




Federal Reserve FOMC statement
Announced target range
Confirms the policy event


Federal Reserve H.15 table
Effective federal-funds and bank prime rates
Documents daily short-rate adjustment


Freddie Mac PMMS archive
Weekly 30- and 15-year mortgage rates
Measures household financing conditions


Census New Residential Sales
July 2026 median new-home sales price
Defines a nationally scaled illustrative scenario



All four pages are public and require no login, CAPTCHA, paywall, or access workaround. The script makes at most one request per source when a cached file is absent, waits before requesting, identifies the academic user agent, and reuses local HTML thereafter. This both limits server load and fixes the source vintage for reproducibility.
Freddie Mac’s September 17 PMMS observation is not a clean post-announcement mortgage rate. The weekly survey summarizes applications received largely from the preceding Thursday through Wednesday, so this observation covers approximately September 10–16, while the FOMC announcement occurred at 2:00 p.m. on September 16. I therefore call it the FOMC-week PMMS rate, not the “after” rate. The comparison below is descriptive and does not identify the causal effect of the announcement.

title: The Hidden Cost of a Rate Hike
section: Finding 1: the transmission was immediate, but not one-for-one
text:
Finding 1: the transmission was immediate, but not one-for-one
The effective federal-funds rate moved from 3.63% to 3.88%, while the bank prime rate moved from 6.75% to 7.00%. These short-term rates followed the 25-basis-point policy move closely.
The 30-year mortgage rate behaved differently. It rose from 6.76% on September 10 to 6.95% on September 17, a 19-basis-point weekly increase. Figure 1 also shows that mortgage rates had been rising before the announcement. That is economically sensible because mortgage rates reflect expected future short rates, long-term yields, and mortgage-backed-security risk:
\[
r_t^{mortgage}
\approx
y_t^{10Y}+\text{MBS spread}_t.
\]


Show the reproducible R code
english_month_breaks <- ymd(sprintf("2026-%02d-01", 1:9))

p1 <- pmms |>
  filter(date >= ymd("2026-01-01"), date <= ymd("2026-09-17")) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, mortgage_30y)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9, color = "#24496e") +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = ymd("2026-09-16"),
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "#b24c3d",
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_point(data = analysis_rates, size = 3.2, color = "#b24c3d") +
  geom_text(
    data = analysis_rates,
    aes(label = percent(mortgage_30y, accuracy = 0.01)),
    vjust = -0.9,
    color = "#8f382d",
    size = 3.6
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 0.1)) +
  scale_x_date(
    breaks = english_month_breaks,
    labels = month.abb[1:9],
    limits = ymd(c("2026-01-01", "2026-09-22")),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.02))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = paste0(
      "The 30-year mortgage rate reached ",
      percent(rate_after, accuracy = 0.01)
    ),
    subtitle = "Weekly national average, January-September 2026",
    x = NULL,
    y = "30-year fixed mortgage rate"
  )

p1
ggsave(
  file.path(figure_dir, "mortgage-rate-trend.png"),
  p1,
  width = 8,
  height = 5,
  dpi = 300
)








Figure 1: Figure 1. Weekly U.S. 30-year fixed mortgage rate. The red points are the September 10 and 17 comparison observations; the dashed line marks the September 16 FOMC decision. Source: Freddie Mac PMMS; author’s calculations.





The figure documents timing, not causality. A 19-basis-point weekly change is not a causal estimate of the FOMC announcement because markets anticipated the meeting and other rate components moved simultaneously. A causal design would require a narrower high-frequency event window and market instruments observed around the exact announcement time.

title: The Hidden Cost of a Rate Hike
section: Finding 2: a small rate change compounds over 360 payments
text:
Finding 2: a small rate change compounds over 360 payments
For loan principal \(L\), monthly rate \(r\), and \(N=360\) payments, monthly principal and interest equal
\[
M=L\frac{r(1+r)^N}{(1+r)^N-1}.
\]
This nonlinear annuity formula converts the observed mortgage-rate change into a household cash-flow effect.


Show the reproducible R code
loan_values <- c(300000, 400000, 500000)

payment_grid <- crossing(
  mortgage_rate = seq(0.04, 0.08, by = 0.0005),
  loan = loan_values
) |>
  mutate(monthly_payment = mortgage_payment(loan, mortgage_rate))

p2 <- ggplot(
  payment_grid,
  aes(mortgage_rate, monthly_payment, color = factor(loan))
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = rate_before,
    linetype = "dotted",
    linewidth = 0.8,
    color = "#555555"
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = rate_after,
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.8,
    color = "#b24c3d"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = rate_before,
    y = max(payment_grid$monthly_payment) * 0.985,
    label = before_label,
    angle = 90,
    hjust = 1,
    vjust = 1.3,
    size = 3.2
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = rate_after,
    y = max(payment_grid$monthly_payment) * 0.985,
    label = after_label,
    angle = 90,
    hjust = 1,
    vjust = -0.4,
    color = "#8f382d",
    size = 3.2
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 0.1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = dollar_format()) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("#3f7d5c", "#c17b31", "#8d4773"),
    breaks = as.character(loan_values),
    labels = dollar(loan_values)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Small rate changes compound over 360 payments",
    subtitle = "Monthly principal and interest by loan size",
    x = "Mortgage rate",
    y = "Monthly payment",
    color = "Loan amount"
  )

p2
ggsave(
  file.path(figure_dir, "payment-curves.png"),
  p2,
  width = 8,
  height = 5,
  dpi = 300
)








Figure 2: Figure 2. Monthly principal and interest for a 30-year fixed mortgage. The dotted and dashed lines mark the observed before and after rates. Taxes, insurance, fees, and maintenance are excluded.





Using the scraped Census median new-home price of $393,800 and a 20% down payment implies a $315,040 mortgage. Monthly principal and interest rise from $2,045 to $2,085: an increase of $40 per month, or $480 per year. In percentage terms, the payment rises by 1.95% even though the mortgage rate rises by only 19 basis points.
Figure 2 also reveals scale exposure. The same rate increase adds more dollars to the payment on a larger loan because the rate applies to a larger principal. This is why highly leveraged buyers are more sensitive to monetary tightening.

title: The Hidden Cost of a Rate Hike
section: Finding 3: fixed-budget buyers lose purchasing power
text:
Finding 3: fixed-budget buyers lose purchasing power
The more decision-relevant calculation holds the monthly budget fixed and solves the annuity formula for the maximum loan:
\[
L_{max}=M\frac{1-(1+r)^{-N}}{r}.
\]
With a 20% down payment, maximum home price is \(L_{max}/0.80\).


Show the reproducible R code
period_levels <- c(before_label, after_label)

budget_results <- crossing(
  monthly_budget = c(2000, 2500, 3000),
  period = period_levels
) |>
  mutate(
    period = factor(period, levels = period_levels),
    rate = if_else(period == before_label, rate_before, rate_after),
    max_home_price = max_loan(monthly_budget, rate) / 0.80
  )

budget_summary <- budget_results |>
  select(monthly_budget, period, max_home_price) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = period, values_from = max_home_price) |>
  mutate(
    dollar_loss = .data[[after_label]] - .data[[before_label]],
    percent_loss = .data[[after_label]] / .data[[before_label]] - 1
  )




Show the reproducible R code
p3 <- ggplot(
  budget_results,
  aes(factor(monthly_budget), max_home_price, fill = period)
) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = dollar(max_home_price, accuracy = 1000)),
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.75),
    vjust = -0.35,
    size = 3.6
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = dollar_format(),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("#7396b8", "#c65d45"),
    breaks = period_levels

  labs(

title: The Hidden Cost of Higher Mortgage Rates
section: Decision rule and stress test
text:
Decision rule and stress test
The observed weekly difference is modest compared with the rate uncertainty a buyer may face between preapproval and closing. A practical decision rule is therefore to choose a home price that remains within the buyer’s all-in budget under a higher-rate scenario, not merely at today’s quoted rate.


Show the reproducible R code
stress_test <- tibble(
  Scenario = c(

title: The Hidden Cost of Higher Mortgage Rates
section: What this analysis can and cannot establish
text:
What this analysis can and cannot establish
The evidence supports a cash-flow scenario, not a causal monetary-policy estimate. PMMS is a national weekly average, and the September 17 observation largely summarizes applications submitted before the September 16 announcement. An individual quote also depends on credit score, loan-to-value ratio, points, geography, and loan type. The Census input is the July 2026 national median for newly built single-family homes, not a September price and not the median for all U.S. housing transactions. Most importantly, comparing two weekly PMMS releases cannot isolate the surprise component of monetary policy from expectations or other news.
A deeper follow-up could merge daily Treasury yields and mortgage-backed-security spreads, separate expected policy from announcement surprises, and compare metro areas with different price levels. That extension would test whether a given rate shock has larger dollar effects in expensive markets and whether changing spreads amplify or absorb policy-rate movements.

title: The Hidden Cost of Higher Mortgage Rates
section: Takeaway
text:
Takeaway
The September episode contains two related but empirically distinct developments: the policy decision mechanically raised short-term benchmark rates, while the FOMC-week PMMS mortgage rate was also higher than the previous week’s reading. Applying that observed weekly difference to a standard amortization model shows how even a modestly higher mortgage rate can reduce the home price supported by a fixed principal-and-interest budget. For buyers, the relevant cost of a house is therefore not its listing price alone; it is the long-term cash-flow commitment jointly created by the price, down payment, and financing rate.

section: Finding 3: a fixed P&I budget supports a lower purchase price at a higher rate
text:
Finding 3: a fixed P&I budget supports a lower purchase price at a higher rate
The more decision-relevant calculation holds the monthly budget fixed and solves the annuity formula for the maximum loan:
\[
L_{max}=M\frac{1-(1+r)^{-N}}{r}.
\]
With a 20% down payment, the home price supported by the assumed principal-and-interest budget is \(L_{max}/0.80\). This calculation assumes the buyer can supply cash equal to 20% of the implied purchase price; it does not impose a separate cash-on-hand constraint.

  period = period_levels

  mutate(

      rate_previous_week,
      rate_fomc_week

section: Research Design
text:
Research Design
The analysis follows a transparent pipeline:

Collect: scrape four public webpages with rvest and cache one dated HTML copy of each page.
Clean: convert table headings into dates, percentage strings into decimals, and price text into a numeric dollar value.
Validate: require the policy and mortgage observations used in the comparison to be present and nonmissing.
Calculate: apply the fixed-rate mortgage annuity formula under explicit assumptions.
Decide: convert the estimates into budget and stress-testing recommendations for prospective buyers.


Sources and ethical access

Measures household financing conditions

July 2026 median new-home sales price
Defines a nationally scaled illustrative scenario



All four pages are public and require no login, CAPTCHA, paywall, or access workaround. The script makes at most one request per source when a cached file is absent, waits before requesting, identifies the academic user agent, and reuses local HTML thereafter. Freddie Mac’s September 17 PMMS observation is not a clean post-announcement mortgage rate. I therefore call it the FOMC-week PMMS rate, not the “after” rate. The comparison below is descriptive and does not identify the causal effect of the announcement.

L_{max}=M\frac{1-(1+r)^{-N}}{r}.
\]
With a 20% down payment, the home price supported by the assumed principal-and-interest budget is \(L_{max}/0.80\). This calculation assumes the buyer can supply cash equal to 20% of the implied purchase price; it does not impose a separate cash-on-hand constraint.

  period = period_levels

  mutate(

  filter(monthly_budget == 2000) |>
  pull(dollar_loss) |>

title: When Young Children Are at Home, Who Is at Work?
text:
Figure 1. Young children, different employment patterns


Employed adults per 100 adults, by recorded sex and youngest own child at home; ages 25–54, 2025.



MenWomen


Source: IPUMS CPS ASEC; author’s weighted estimates. Population and coverage notes.



Chart notes


Labels show weighted employment rates. The denominator is all adults in each group. “No minor child” includes adults whose own children are absent or aged 18 or older; it does not mean never a parent. Older-child groups are different households, not the young-child group followed over time.



A workday does not always end when a child needs collecting. Someone has to leave, arrange help or pay for care that covers the gap. For a family with a young child, fitting those hours together can matter as much as finding a vacancy.
The employment comparison differs by sex. Women living with a young child have lower employment than women with no own minor child at home, a gap of -9.9 percentage points. For men, the corresponding gap is +12.7 percentage points. One overall figure for parents would obscure that comparison.
How does employment differ for women and men living with young children? And does the difference reflect participation in the labor force, with the same pattern remaining after age and education adjustment? The comparison concerns Americans aged 25–54 in 2025, with a young child defined as the youngest own child at home aged 0–5.1, 2, 8


Among women in the young-child group, 67.7% are employed, against 77.5% among women with no own minor child at home. The equivalent figures for men are 93.6% and 80.9%. These percentages count adults with a job out of all adults in each group.3
Figure 1 sets that comparison beside households with older children. A rate of 80% means about 80 adults in work per 100 in the group. A gap of ten percentage points means a difference of ten employed adults per 100, rather than a ten per cent relative change.4
For households, access to paid work can affect the ability to earn or withstand a lost wage. But the chart does not measure pay, hours or financial hardship. It also cannot show how a particular family’s employment changed after a birth: each bar describes different people at one point in time.



Having no job is not always counted as unemployment. The labor force includes adults who are employed and those who are unemployed; people neither working nor meeting the unemployment definition are outside it. This distinction separates participation in paid work from success in finding it.3
Women living with a young child have a participation rate of 69.8%, compared with 80.3% in the reference group. Among participants, unemployment is 3.0% and 3.5%, respectively.


Figure 2. Having no job is not always unemployment


Each bar divides all adults in its group between work, job search and nonparticipation.



EmployedUnemployedOutside the labor force


Source: IPUMS CPS ASEC; author’s weighted estimates. Population and coverage notes.



Chart notes


The segments sum to 100% of all adults. The unemployed segment is not the unemployment rate, whose denominator is labor-force participants. Outside the labor force does not identify childcare as the reason for nonparticipation. Men and women use the same scale.



An accounting breakdown assigns -10.2 percentage points of the women’s employment gap to participation differences and +0.3 percentage points to unemployment differences. The participation component is larger in absolute size than the unemployment component. The two components add to the observed employment gap; they do not identify what caused it.5
For employers and policymakers, that distinction changes the question. A participation gap prompts examination of whether paid work can fit household circumstances. An unemployment gap concerns job finding among those already in the labor force. The bars cannot distinguish care responsibilities from health, preferences or other reasons for not participating.



Adults living with young children may differ in age and qualifications from the reference group. A weighted linear probability model compares their employment while allowing for three age bands and whether they hold a bachelor’s degree. It also allows the child-group association to differ for women and men.6
For women, adjustment changes the gap from -9.9 percentage points to -10.7 percentage points. For men, it changes from +12.7 percentage points to +11.2 percentage points. Both associations retain their direction: broad age and education differences do not explain away the pattern.


Figure 3. Does adjustment change the employment divide?


Young-child employment minus employment with no minor child, in percentage points.



Observed weighted gapAdjusted for age and degree status


Source: Author’s weighted linear probability model; IPUMS CPS ASEC.



Chart notes


Positive bars indicate higher employment in the young-child group, negative bars lower employment. Both panels use the same signed scale and zero line. Adjusted 95% confidence intervals appear in the table below. Adjustment is a conditional association, not the effect of having a child.



The model’s outcome is one when an adult is employed and zero otherwise. Its coefficients therefore describe differences in the probability of employment; multiplying a contrast by 100 expresses it in percentage points. The specification is:

\[
E_i=\alpha+\beta F_i+\sum_g\gamma_g C_{ig}
+\sum_g\delta_g(F_i C_{ig})+\boldsymbol{\theta}'A_i+\lambda B_i+u_i.
\]

Here \(F_i\) identifies women, \(C_{ig}\) child-age groups, \(A_i\) age bands and \(B_i\) degree status. The no-minor-child group is the reference. The young-child contrast is \(\gamma_{\text{young}}\) for men and \(\gamma_{\text{young}}+\delta_{\text{young}}\) for women. The table reports those contrasts and the difference between them.6, 7












Comparison
Observed gap (pp)
Adjusted gap (pp)
Adjusted 95% interval (pp)




Men: young child vs no minor child
+12.7
+11.2
[+10.1, +12.4]


Women: young child vs no minor child
-9.9
-10.7
[-12.3, -9.1]


Women minus men: difference between associations
-22.5
-21.9
[-23.9, -20.0]






The adjusted women’s interval is below zero and the men’s is above zero. The difference between the adjusted associations is -21.9 percentage points; its interval is below zero. An interval crossing zero leaves the direction of that particular association uncertain.
Adjustment makes the comparison more specific, but it leaves partner earnings, care availability and selection into parenthood unaccounted for. The model describes an employment association among broadly comparable adults. It does not estimate what having a child would do to an individual’s job prospects.



The participation breakdown and adjusted comparison locate the employment difference more precisely than a single parenthood average. They do not establish which constraint caused it or how much a particular policy would change it.
Employers examining retention can assess whether schedules, leave and return-to-work arrangements fit the needs of staff with care responsibilities. Policymakers evaluating childcare provision should examine participation alongside unemployment and test whether support reaches adults who want paid work. These are priorities for assessment, rather than remedies whose effects this model has measured.
If more reliable care and workable schedules enable additional adults to participate, employment could rise without a large fall in unemployment. Testing that possibility requires evidence over time and a credible evaluation. This cross-section cannot forecast employment or household income.



Young children at home are associated with different employment patterns for women and men. Their observed gaps relative to adults with no own minor child are -9.9 percentage points and +12.7 percentage points, respectively. Participation helps describe the women’s comparison; age and education adjustment changes the gaps to -10.7 percentage points and +11.2 percentage points.
The practical implication is to examine access to paid work as well as job finding. Work and care arrangements deserve closer scrutiny, while uncertainty and unmeasured household circumstances limit conclusions about causes and remedies.





 Population, sources and coverage. Author’s analysis of the 2025 IPUMS CPS ASEC, sample cps2025_03s, ages 25–54 with valid analysis variables and positive ASECWT. This is a single cross-section, not a truncated 2024–2026 series. Downloaded person records include ages and cases outside the analytic sample; sample_audit.csv documents selection. CPS is a household survey; ASEC is its annual social and economic supplement.
 Children and recorded sex. YNGCH describes the youngest own biological, adopted or stepchild at home. “No minor child” includes no own child present or a youngest own child aged 18 or older. It does not identify adults who have never been parents. Recorded sex is not a measure of gender identity.
 Employment, participation and unemployment. Employment divides employed adults by all adults in the group. Participation divides employed plus unemployed adults by all adults. Unemployment divides unemployed adults by labor-force participants; the classification includes people on temporary layoff under the applicable definition. Figure 2 instead divides every status by all adults.
 Percentage points and household implications. 80% minus 70% is ten percentage points, not a ten per cent relative increase. A group employment-rate difference is not a count of individuals who left work after childbirth. Household-income, hours and care mechanisms discussed in the article are interpretations to investigate, not additional estimates from these figures.
 Participation breakdown. Employment equals participation multiplied by one minus unemployment. With \(L\) for participation, \(U\) for unemployment, \(y\) for young-child households and \(n\) for the reference, the employment gap is \(100(L_y-L_n)(1-U_n)-100L_y(U_y-U_n)\). The two components use the reference unemployment rate and the young-child participation rate. This accounting identity is not a causal decomposition.
 Model and comparisons. The specification is employed ~ sex * child_group + age_band + college. References are men, no minor child, ages 25–34 and below bachelor’s degree. Age bands are 25–34, 35–44 and 45–54. The linear model can produce fitted probabilities outside zero and one; model diagnostics record that limitation. Adjusted bars are coefficient contrasts at common controls, not observed employment rates.
 Weights and uncertainty. ASECWT supplies person weights. Uncertainty uses all 160 REPWTP person replicate weights, successive-difference replication and mse=TRUE. Contrasts use t(159) intervals and account for covariance between main and interaction terms. See IPUMS replicate-weight guidance. Observed gaps have no intervals in this table; the displayed intervals refer to adjusted contrasts. Full parameters and diagnostics are exported on a microdata run.
 Execution and publication status. Execution mode: original microdata re-estimated in this run. A reference preview permits inspection of the draft. A new raw-data run and editorial review are required before final publication.





The analysis code is included in the accompanying project. The standalone repository uses the following structure. Generated data and result files appear after a successful run:

To reproduce the figures, open the website’s RStudio project and place this post under blog/posts/post3/, retaining the folder structure. Keep the corresponding IPUMS CPS extract and its XML dictionary together in a private folder. Set BLOG3_DDI_PATH to the dictionary path if using an existing extract; otherwise the first run requests the extract through the API. Input placement and key setup are documented in README.md.

title: Tiny Shoes, Big Questions
section: Data and analysis pipeline
text:
Data and analysis pipeline
The data do not arrive as a ready-made table of “mothers with toddlers versus fathers with toddlers.” The R code above asks the IPUMS API for the 2025 ASEC person-level extract (cps2025_03s) in CSV format. IPUMS sends a compressed CSV and an XML data dictionary (DDI). The first render downloads them to a private cache outside this website; later renders reuse a complete download. The extract request is saved there too, so an interrupted download can resume without asking IPUMS to build another extract.








IPUMS variable
What it supplies
How this article uses it




YEAR, AGE
Survey year and age
Confirm 2025; keep ages 25–54


SEX
CPS recorded sex
Compare groups labelled women and men


YNGCH
Age of youngest own child living in the household
Define the child-age groups


EMPSTAT
Employment and labor-force status
Build employment, participation, and unemployment measures


EDUC
Highest educational attainment
Separate bachelor’s degree or higher from below bachelor’s in the model


ASECWT
ASEC person weight
Estimate population rates and fit the weighted model


REPWTP1–REPWTP160
ASEC person replicate weights
Compute survey-based uncertainty, including error bars



The next code block creates four mutually exclusive groups: no resident minor own child, youngest own child 0–5, 6–12, or 13–17. It keeps adults ages 25–54 with a known employment status and positive person weight, excludes unknown education (EDUC = 999), and converts employment into a 0/1 indicator. Someone without a resident minor child may still be a parent. The code then computes weighted rates separately for each sex and child group.


Show the R code
# Step 5: recode child age, employment and controls; retain eligible adults.
# EMPSTAT general code 1 = employed; 2 = unemployed; 3 = not in labor force.
# YNGCH 99 = no identified own child living in the household.
# EDUC 999 = missing or unknown. EDUC 000 may also mean no schooling, so retain it.
cps <- cps_raw |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    sex = factor(as.numeric(SEX), levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("Men", "Women")),
    child_group = dplyr::case_when(
      YNGCH == 99 | YNGCH >= 18 ~ "no_minor",
      YNGCH >= 0 & YNGCH <= 5 ~ "age0_5",
      YNGCH >= 6 & YNGCH <= 12 ~ "age6_12",
      YNGCH >= 13 & YNGCH <= 17 ~ "age13_17",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    child_group = factor(child_group,
                         levels = c("no_minor", "age0_5", "age6_12", "age13_17")),
    status = floor(as.numeric(EMPSTAT) / 10),
    employed = as.numeric(status == 1),
    labor_force = as.numeric(status %in% c(1, 2)),
    unemployed = as.numeric(status == 2),
    age_band = factor(dplyr::case_when(
      AGE <= 34 ~ "25–34", AGE <= 44 ~ "35–44", TRUE ~ "45–54"
    ), levels = c("25–34", "35–44", "45–54")),
    college = factor(ifelse(EDUC >= 111, "BA or higher", "Below BA"),
                     levels = c("Below BA", "BA or higher"))
  ) |>
  dplyr::filter(AGE >= 25, AGE <= 54, !is.na(sex), !is.na(child_group),
                status %in% c(1, 2, 3), !is.na(EDUC), EDUC != 999,
                !is.na(ASECWT), ASECWT > 0)
if (!nrow(cps)) stop("No eligible records: inspect IPUMS variable codes.")
# Step 6: make the ASEC person-weighted survey design with all 160 replicates.
design <- srvyr::as_survey_rep(
  cps, weight = ASECWT, repweights = dplyr::matches("^REPWTP[0-9]+$"),
  type = "successive-difference", mse = TRUE
)
# Step 7: estimate eight group rates and their design-based confidence intervals.
rates <- design |>
  dplyr::group_by(sex, child_group) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    employment = srvyr::survey_mean(employed, vartype = "ci", na.rm = TRUE),
    participation = srvyr::survey_mean(labor_force, vartype = "ci", na.rm = TRUE),
    unemployment = srvyr::survey_ratio(unemployed, labor_force,
                                        vartype = "ci", na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  as.data.frame()
readr::write_csv(rates, file.path(derived_dir, "weighted_rates.csv"))
pick_rate <- function(s, g, col = "employment") {
  row <- rates[rates$sex == s & rates$child_group == g, , drop = FALSE]
  if (nrow(row) != 1L) stop("An expected group is missing: ", s, ", ", g)
  as.numeric(row[[col]])
}
e_w_young <- pick_rate("Women", "age0_5")
e_m_young <- pick_rate("Men", "age0_5")
e_w_none <- pick_rate("Women", "no_minor")
e_m_none <- pick_rate("Men", "no_minor")
women_gap <- 100 * (e_w_young - e_w_none)
men_gap <- 100 * (e_m_young - e_m_none)
fmt_pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * x)
fmt_pp <- function(x) sprintf("%+.1f percentage points", x)


The API extract contained 142,125 person records; after the stated sample restrictions, 54,607 records enter the analysis. These are sample counts, not estimates of the population size. The employment rate is the weighted share working; participation is the weighted share working or looking for work; unemployment divides weighted job seekers by the weighted labor force. All three rates are stored in data/derived/weighted_rates.csv.

title: Tiny Shoes, Big Questions
section: 1. First, what do the employment rates say?
text:
1. First, what do the employment rates say?
The CPS interviews a sample, so a respondent does not necessarily represent the same number of people as another respondent. We calculate each group’s employment rate with the ASEC person weight, ASECWT, rather than counting sample records equally. The slim vertical lines in the figure show 95% confidence intervals calculated with the survey’s person replicate weights.


Show the R code
# Step 8: plot and save weighted employment rates and their intervals.
labels <- c(no_minor = "No resident minor child", age0_5 = "Youngest child 0–5",
            age6_12 = "Youngest child 6–12", age13_17 = "Youngest child 13–17")
palette <- c(Men = "#147d87", Women = "#db6b54")
theme_blog <- function() ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(),
                 plot.title.position = "plot", legend.position = "top",
                 plot.title = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold", color = "#17304b"))
p1 <- ggplot2::ggplot(rates,
                      ggplot2::aes(x = child_group, y = 100 * employment,
                                   color = sex)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(position = ggplot2::position_dodge(width = .5), size = 3) +
  ggplot2::geom_errorbar(
    ggplot2::aes(ymin = 100 * employment_low, ymax = 100 * employment_upp),
    position = ggplot2::position_dodge(width = .5), width = .15
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_discrete(labels = labels) +
  ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = palette) +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "Employment across household stages",
                x = NULL, y = "Employed (%)", color = NULL) +
  theme_blog() +
  ggplot2::theme(axis.text.x = ggplot2::element_text(angle = 18, hjust = 1))
ggplot2::ggsave(file.path(figure_dir, "figure1_employment.png"), p1,
                width = 9, height = 5, dpi = 200)
p1








Figure 1: Weighted employment-to-population ratios for adults ages 25–54. Source: IPUMS CPS, 2025 ASEC. Error bars are 95% design-based confidence intervals.





Among adults with a youngest resident child ages 0–5, the weighted employment rate is 67.7% for women and 93.6% for men. Relative to adults with no resident minor child, the within-sex differences are -9.9 percentage points for women and +12.7 percentage points for men. These are descriptive comparisons: the household groups may differ in age, education, and circumstances we cannot measure here.

title: Tiny Shoes, Big Questions
section: 2. Not working is not always unemployment
text:
2. Not working is not always unemployment
An adult who is not working may be looking for work, or may be outside the labor force. That distinction changes the interpretation of the first chart. Participation is the share of everyone in the group who works or is seeking work. Unemployment is the share of labor-force members who are seeking work without a job. Notice that the two panels have different vertical scales and denominators; compare patterns within each panel.


Show the R code
# Step 9: plot and save labor-force participation and unemployment.
panels <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  dplyr::transmute(rates, sex, child_group,
                   measure = "Labor-force participation", value = 100 * participation),
  dplyr::transmute(rates, sex, child_group,
                   measure = "Unemployment among the labor force", value = 100 * unemployment)
)
p2 <- ggplot2::ggplot(panels,
                      ggplot2::aes(x = child_group, y = value,
                                   color = sex, group = sex)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = .8) + ggplot2::geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ measure, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_discrete(labels = labels) +
  ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = palette) +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "Not employed does not always mean unemployed",
                x = NULL, y = "Percent (panel-specific denominator)", color = NULL) +
  theme_blog() +
  ggplot2::theme(axis.text.x = ggplot2::element_text(angle = 18, hjust = 1))
ggplot2::ggsave(file.path(figure_dir, "figure2_labor_force.png"), p2,
                width = 9, height = 7, dpi = 200)
p2








Figure 2: Two complementary labor-market measures. Participation divides by all adults in a group; unemployment divides only by adults in its labor force. Source: IPUMS CPS, 2025 ASEC.







Show the R code
lf_w_young <- pick_rate("Women", "age0_5", "participation")
lf_w_none <- pick_rate("Women", "no_minor", "participation")
u_w_young <- pick_rate("Women", "age0_5", "unemployment")
u_w_none <- pick_rate("Women", "no_minor", "unemployment")
participation_sentence <- if (lf_w_young < lf_w_none) {
  "is lower"
} else if (lf_w_young > lf_w_none) {
  "is higher"
} else {
  "is equal"
}


For women with a youngest resident child ages 0–5, participation is lower than among women with no resident minor child (69.8% versus 80.3%). The corresponding unemployment rates are 3.0% and 3.5%. These measures help locate the descriptive source of an employment-rate difference. They cannot tell us why a person is outside the labor force.

title: Tiny Shoes, Big Questions
section: 3. What if we compare similar ages and education?
text:
3. What if we compare similar ages and education?
The first chart compares real population groups, but those groups may have different age and education mixes. A survey-weighted linear probability model compares employment across child groups while accounting for age band and education, with a separate young-child contrast for women and men. Think of it as checking whether our first comparison changes when we make those two measured characteristics more alike. The result is still an association.


Show the R code
# Step 10: estimate adjusted within-sex gaps and their difference.
model <- survey::svyglm(
  employed ~ sex * child_group + age_band + college,
  design = design, family = stats::gaussian()
)
b <- stats::coef(model)
V <- stats::vcov(model)
ci_critical <- stats::qt(0.975, df = 159) # 160 replicates imply 159 design df.
men_term <- "child_groupage0_5"
interaction_term <- "sexWomen:child_groupage0_5"
stopifnot(all(c(men_term, interaction_term) %in% names(b)))
contrast <- function(label, terms) {
  cvec <- stats::setNames(rep(0, length(b)), names(b))
  cvec[terms] <- 1

title: Tiny Shoes, Big Questions
section: What should we take away?
text:
What should we take away?
The youngest child’s age and employment can be related in different ways for women and men. We have documented that relationship in population-weighted comparisons, checked whether participation and unemployment tell the same story, and tested how much the comparison changes after accounting for age and education. The strongest honest conclusion is about patterns among households, not what any particular child did to a parent’s career. A toddler may rearrange the morning schedule; these data alone cannot identify the counterfactual career path.






Reading the evidence carefully



The CPS variable SEX records survey categories labelled women and men here; it is not a measure of gender identity. YNGCH covers co-resident children identified by IPUMS family links. The model is descriptive and does not establish a causal effect of parenthood.

title: The employment divide around young children
section: The survey and the comparison
text:
The survey and the comparison
The unit is a person, aged 25 to 54. IPUMS’s YNGCH identifies the youngest own child living in that person’s household; the definition includes biological, step and adopted children. The reference group has no own child under 18 living at home. It can include parents with adult children or children living elsewhere, so it should not be called a childless group.
The API request obtains the 2025 ASEC person extract (cps2025_03s) and its XML dictionary. The first run stores the person records in a private cache outside the website; subsequent runs reuse the download. We exclude missing employment or education responses and records with nonpositive person weights.







Input
Role in the analysis




AGE, SEX, YNGCH
Define ages 25 to 54, recorded sex and youngest resident child groups


EMPSTAT, EDUC
Determine labor market status and education category


ASECWT
Weight each observation for population estimates


REPWTP1 to REPWTP160
Calculate sampling uncertainty using the ASEC replicate weights



We compare four groups: no resident minor child; youngest resident child aged 0 to 5, 6 to 12 or 13 to 17. The following code creates the variables, survey design and weighted group rates.


Show R code
# Step 5: recode child age, employment and controls; retain eligible adults.
# EMPSTAT general code 1 = employed; 2 = unemployed; 3 = not in labor force.
# YNGCH 99 = no identified own child living in the household.
# EDUC 999 = missing or unknown. EDUC 000 may also mean no schooling, so retain it.
cps <- cps_raw |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    sex = factor(as.numeric(SEX), levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("Men", "Women")),
    child_group = dplyr::case_when(
      YNGCH == 99 | YNGCH >= 18 ~ "no_minor",
      YNGCH >= 0 & YNGCH <= 5 ~ "age0_5",
      YNGCH >= 6 & YNGCH <= 12 ~ "age6_12",
      YNGCH >= 13 & YNGCH <= 17 ~ "age13_17",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    child_group = factor(child_group,
                         levels = c("no_minor", "age0_5", "age6_12", "age13_17")),
    status = floor(as.numeric(EMPSTAT) / 10),
    employed = as.numeric(status == 1),
    labor_force = as.numeric(status %in% c(1, 2)),
    unemployed = as.numeric(status == 2),
    age_band = factor(dplyr::case_when(
      AGE <= 34 ~ "25-34", AGE <= 44 ~ "35-44", TRUE ~ "45-54"
    ), levels = c("25-34", "35-44", "45-54")),
    college = factor(ifelse(EDUC >= 111, "BA or higher", "Below BA"),
                     levels = c("Below BA", "BA or higher"))
  ) |>
  dplyr::filter(AGE >= 25, AGE <= 54, !is.na(sex), !is.na(child_group),
                status %in% c(1, 2, 3), !is.na(EDUC), EDUC != 999,
                !is.na(ASECWT), ASECWT > 0)
if (!nrow(cps)) stop("No eligible records: inspect IPUMS variable codes.")
# Step 6: make the ASEC person-weighted survey design with all 160 replicates.
design <- srvyr::as_survey_rep(
  cps, weight = ASECWT, repweights = dplyr::matches("^REPWTP[0-9]+$"),
  type = "successive-difference", mse = TRUE
)
# Step 7: estimate eight group rates and their design-based confidence intervals.
rates <- design |>
  dplyr::group_by(sex, child_group) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    employment = srvyr::survey_mean(employed, vartype = "ci", na.rm = TRUE),
    participation = srvyr::survey_mean(labor_force, vartype = "ci", na.rm = TRUE),
    unemployment = srvyr::survey_ratio(unemployed, labor_force,
                                        vartype = "ci", na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  as.data.frame()
readr::write_csv(rates, file.path(derived_dir, "weighted_rates.csv"))
pick_rate <- function(s, g, col = "employment") {
  row <- rates[rates$sex == s & rates$child_group == g, , drop = FALSE]
  if (nrow(row) != 1L) stop("An expected group is missing: ", s, ", ", g)
  as.numeric(row[[col]])
}

e_m_young <- pick_rate("Men", "age0_5")
e_w_none <- pick_rate("Women", "no_minor")
e_m_none <- pick_rate("Men", "no_minor")
women_gap <- 100 * (e_w_young - e_w_none)
men_gap <- 100 * (e_m_young - e_m_none)
fmt_pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * x)
fmt_pp <- function(x) sprintf("%+.1f percentage points", x)
# Consistency check: employment = participation * (1 - unemployment).
stopifnot(max(abs(rates$employment - rates$participation *
                    (1 - rates$unemployment))) < 1e-8)

What lies behind the employment rates?
Employment is one of three possible states in this classification. An adult can also be unemployed and seeking work, or outside the labor force. title: The employment divide around young children
section: Does the contrast survive basic adjustment?
text:
Does the contrast survive basic adjustment?
The household groups need not have the same age or education mix. We fit a survey-weighted linear probability model for being employed, including recorded sex, child-age group, their interaction, age band and whether the person has a bachelor’s degree. In plain terms, the model asks whether the contrast remains when we compare people in the same broad age and education categories. The interaction asks whether the young-child contrast is different for women and men. This model cannot hold constant unobserved income, partnership, child care access or preferences.


Show R code

  employed ~ sex * child_group + age_band + college,
  design = design, family = stats::gaussian()
)

interaction_term <- "sexWomen:child_groupage0_5"

contrast <- function(label, terms) {

  cvec[terms] <- 1
  estimate <- sum(cvec * b)
  se <- sqrt(as.numeric(t(cvec) %*% V %*% cvec))
  data.frame(group = label, estimate_pp = 100 * estimate,
             lower_pp = 100 * (estimate - ci_critical * se),
             upper_pp = 100 * (estimate + ci_critical * se), se_pp = 100 * se)
}

title: The employment divide around young children
section: The economic reading
text:
The economic reading
The striking feature of these data is the opposite sign of the young-child comparison for women and men. For women, lower employment accompanies lower labor force participation, rather than higher unemployment among participants. For men, both employment and participation are higher in the young-child group than in the reference group. Broad age and education controls leave that contrast in place.
Several stories could produce these patterns: different division of paid and unpaid work, selection into parenthood, partnership and household income, or constraints around child care. The CPS snapshot cannot separate those mechanisms. The result is a well-measured description of who is working across household types, and a reason to ask better questions about the choices and constraints behind it.

The employment rate is the ASECWT-weighted share employed within each sex and child group. Participation is the weighted share employed or unemployed; unemployment is the weighted number unemployed divided by the weighted labor force. The code checks that employment equals participation multiplied by one minus unemployment (up to rounding). The model is a linear probability model with sex-by-child-group interactions. The 160 ASEC person replicate weights and the survey design supply standard errors and confidence intervals. SEX is the CPS recorded sex variable and does not measure gender identity.

title: Young children at home and the employment divide
section: Does age and education adjustment change the picture?
text:
Does age and education adjustment change the picture?
The groups differ in more than family circumstances. For a descriptive check, I estimate a survey-weighted linear probability model. The outcome is one if a person is employed and zero otherwise. Let \(F_i\) indicate a woman, \(C_{ig}\) indicate the youngest-child group \(g\) (relative to no minor child at home), \(A_i\) denote age-band indicators and \(B_i\) indicate a bachelor’s degree or higher. The estimated equation is
\[
\Pr(E_i=1 \mid F_i,C_i,A_i,B_i)
= \alpha + \beta F_i + \sum_g \gamma_g C_{ig}
+ \sum_g \delta_g(F_i C_{ig}) + \boldsymbol{\theta}' A_i + \lambda B_i.
\]
For the 0-to-5 group, \(\gamma_{0-5}\) is the adjusted difference for men; \(\gamma_{0-5}+\delta_{0-5}\) is the difference for women; and \(\delta_{0-5}\) is the difference between those two differences. The reference person is a man aged 25 to 34, without a bachelor’s degree and without an own minor child at home. Model coefficients are percentage-point changes when multiplied by 100, not percentage changes.


Show R code
model <- survey::svyglm(
  employed ~ sex * child_group + age_band + college,
  design = design, family = stats::gaussian()
)
b <- stats::coef(model)
V <- stats::vcov(model)
ci_critical <- stats::qt(.975, df = 159) # 160 person replicates, 159 design df.
men_term <- "child_groupage0_5"
interaction_term <- "sexWomen:child_groupage0_5"
stopifnot(all(c(men_term, interaction_term) %in% names(b)))
contrast <- function(label, terms) {
  cvec <- stats::setNames(rep(0, length(b)), names(b))
  cvec[terms] <- 1
  estimate <- sum(cvec * b)
  se <- sqrt(as.numeric(t(cvec) %*% V %*% cvec))
  data.frame(group = label, estimate_pp = 100 * estimate,
             lower_pp = 100 * (estimate - ci_critical * se),
             upper_pp = 100 * (estimate + ci_critical * se), se_pp = 100 * se)
}
adjusted <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  contrast("Men", men_term),
  contrast("Women", c(men_term, interaction_term)),
  contrast("Women minus men", interaction_term)
)
readr::write_csv(adjusted, file.path(derived_dir, "adjusted_gaps.csv"))
capture.output(summary(model), file = file.path(derived_dir, "model_summary.txt"))
capture.output(sessionInfo(), file = file.path(derived_dir, "session_info.txt"))

adj_m <- adjusted$estimate_pp[adjusted$group == "Men"]

title: When Young Children Are at Home, Who Is at Work?
text:
Young children at home are associated with different employment patterns for women and men. Their observed gaps relative to adults with no own minor child are -9.9 percentage points and +12.7 percentage points, respectively. Participation helps describe the women’s comparison; age and education adjustment changes the gaps to -10.7 percentage points and +11.2 percentage points.
The practical implication is to examine access to paid work as well as job finding. Work and care arrangements deserve closer scrutiny, while uncertainty and unmeasured household circumstances limit conclusions about causes and remedies.

Data, definitions and replication

Data note. The API downloads the full 2025 CPS Annual Social and Economic Supplement person extract, including children and older adults. It contains 142,125 unweighted person records. Person replicate weights for survey uncertainty

= \alpha + \beta F_i + \sum_g \gamma_g C_{ig}
+ \sum_g \delta_g(F_i C_{ig}) + \boldsymbol{\theta}' A_i + \lambda B_i.
\]
For the 0-to-5 group, \(\gamma_{0-5}\) is the adjusted difference for men; \(\gamma_{0-5}+\delta_{0-5}\) is the difference for women; and \(\delta_{0-5}\) is the difference between those two differences. The reference person is a man aged 25 to 34, without a bachelor’s degree and without an own minor child at home. Model coefficients are percentage-point changes when multiplied by 100, not percentage changes.

  design = design, family = stats::gaussian()

interaction_term <- "sexWomen:child_groupage0_5"

  se <- sqrt(as.numeric(t(cvec) %*% V %*% cvec))
  data.frame(group = label, estimate_pp = 100 * estimate,
             lower_pp = 100 * (estimate - ci_critical * se),
             upper_pp = 100 * (estimate + ci_critical * se), se_pp = 100 * se)
}
adjusted <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  contrast("Men", men_term),
  contrast("Women", c(men_term, interaction_term)),
  contrast("Women minus men", interaction_term)
)

title: Inflation and Jobs: A Trade-off That Kept Changing
text:
Figure 1. Unemployment surged first. Inflation followed.


Monthly rates, January 2019 to August 2026; both panels use the same scale.



Annual inflationUnemploymentOctober 2025 unavailable


Source: BLS via FRED; author’s calculations. Coverage and data notes.



Chart notes


The panels share a calendar and a 0-16% scale. Inflation is a price-index change; unemployment is a labor-force share. Endpoint labels refer to the latest common month. Lines break across missing October 2025 observations; the gap is not a fall in either rate.



The steep fall in US inflation after its 2022 peak came with a surprisingly small rise in unemployment. Through December 2024, annual price growth slowed by 6.2 percentage points, while the unemployment rate increased by just 0.5 points.
That outcome challenges the idea that bringing inflation down must require a severe jobs downturn. But the latest readings complicate the picture: by August 2026, inflation was higher than at the end of 2024, while unemployment was unchanged between those endpoints.
For households, relief at the checkout matters alongside dependable work. How have inflation and unemployment evolved together, and did falling inflation come with a sharp rise in unemployment? Since 2019, their relationship has shifted repeatedly, first during the pandemic shock and then as the economy recovered.


In February 2020, unemployment stood at 3.5%. Two months later, it had reached 14.8%, while annual inflation fell to 0.3%. The immediate strain on household budgets came from lost earnings, even as price increases slowed.
Inflation measures the rise in consumer prices; unemployment measures the share of the labor force without work and seeking it.1, 2 One erodes what earnings can buy. The other signals how many people lack a job.
As employment recovered, the pressure shifted. By June 2022, unemployment had fallen to 3.6%, but annual inflation had climbed to 9.1%. More people could earn and spend again, yet rising bills absorbed some of that gain unless incomes kept pace.
Losing work can force households to cut spending, weakening business sales and incentives to hire or invest. Recovering employment can support consumption, but a larger pay packet provides less relief when prices rise quickly.5 The two rates describe different strains on living standards; neither tells the whole story.



The familiar Phillips curve links inflation with pressure in the labor market: when workers become harder to find, wages and prices may face upward pressure.3 The US experience shows why that relationship cannot be read as a fixed rule.
In February 2020, unemployment was 3.5% and inflation 2.3%. In June 2022, unemployment was almost identical, at 3.6%, while inflation was roughly four times as high.


Figure 2. Almost the same unemployment, nearly four times the inflation


February 2020 and June 2022 had similar unemployment rates, but sharply different inflation.



Jan 2019-Feb 2020Mar 2020-Jun 2022Jul 2022-Dec 2024Jan 2025 onward


Source: BLS via FRED; author’s calculations. Coverage and data notes.



Chart notes


Each dot represents a month. The gray line connects consecutive observations chronologically, with a break across October 2025; it is not a fitted Phillips curve. White circles mark selected monthly checkpoints. The colors identify descriptive periods, not estimated structural breaks. Other influences are not held constant.



Low unemployment alone cannot explain that difference. Bernanke and Blanchard’s research on pandemic inflation points to commodity-price shocks and demand shifts against constrained supply as drivers of the initial surge, with tight labor markets adding more persistent pressure.7
The monthly path reflects an economy responding to several shocks. It does not isolate the effect of stronger hiring on prices or measure a Phillips curve with those other influences held constant.



The retreat from the inflation peak was markedly different from the pandemic collapse. Between June 2022 and December 2024, inflation fell from 9.1% to 2.9%, while unemployment rose from 3.6% to 4.1%.
That combination supports part of the case for a soft landing: substantial disinflation accompanied relatively limited deterioration in the labor market.4 It does not establish the contribution of interest rates, or erase the losses borne by workers who became unemployed.


Figure 3. Inflation’s retreat brought a modest rise in unemployment


From June 2022 to December 2024, inflation fell 6.2 points while unemployment rose 0.5 points.



Change in inflationChange in unemploymentLeft: decrease; right: increase


Source: BLS via FRED; author’s calculations. Changes in percentage points between named months.



Chart notes


Each bar subtracts the starting rate from the ending rate. The intervals differ in length. Bars represent endpoint differences, not period averages, cumulative price increases or estimated policy effects. A zero unemployment change between endpoints does not imply no movement within the interval.



The improvement did not continue at the same pace. By August 2026, inflation was 3.4%, above its December 2024 reading, while unemployment remained at 4.1%. Stable unemployment between those dates did not imply an uninterrupted decline in price pressures.
The next adjustment will depend partly on how the labor market cools. Research by Crust, Lansing and Petrosky-Nadeau describes a possible path through fewer vacancies rather than sharply higher unemployment, provided inflation expectations remain stable.8 Even then, fewer openings can make finding work harder.
Policymakers should watch hiring, vacancies, participation and wage growth relative to productivity alongside inflation. Uncertain policy delays strengthen the case for weighing several indicators together.9 Further relief would require easing price pressures while employment and purchasing power hold up; renewed supply disruptions or weaker demand could make that balance harder to sustain.



Inflation and unemployment did not follow a fixed trade-off. From June 2022 to December 2024, inflation fell by 6.2 percentage points while unemployment rose by just 0.5 points. By August 2026, however, inflation had edged higher again, showing that progress was uneven.
The next test is whether price pressures can ease while jobs and real incomes hold up. Policymakers should watch hiring and purchasing power alongside headline rates: for households, lasting relief means both manageable bills and dependable earnings.





Consumer prices, CPI and annual inflation. Consumer prices are what households pay for goods and services. The Consumer Price Index summarizes changes in a representative expenditure-weighted basket; it does not describe every household’s spending pattern. Annual, or year-on-year, inflation is 100 times (the current CPI divided by its value 12 calendar months earlier, minus one). Lower positive inflation means prices rise more slowly, not that prices fall. The series is CPIAUCNS, the BLS all-items CPI for urban consumers, not seasonally adjusted.


Unemployment, the labor force and participation. The labor force includes employed and unemployed people in the civilian noninstitutional population age 16 and older. Unemployed people generally must be available for work and have actively searched during the previous four weeks; those awaiting recall from temporary layoff may qualify without searching. The unemployment rate divides unemployed people by the labor force, not the entire population. Labor-force participation is the share of the relevant population in the labor force. People neither working nor seeking work are generally outside it. See BLS definitions. UNRATE is seasonally adjusted. A falling unemployment rate can reflect employment growth, participation changes, or both.


Phillips curve, labor-market tightness and expectations. The Phillips curve describes a conditional relationship between inflation and labor-market slack. Its familiar downward-sloping version links lower unemployment with higher inflation while holding other influences constant. Tightness concerns the difficulty employers face finding workers, often assessed using vacancies relative to unemployed workers. Inflation expectations are beliefs about future price increases. Supply shocks, expectations and changing labor-market conditions can alter the observed relationship. Figure 2 does not fit a structural Phillips curve or test whether such a conditional relationship exists.


Percentage points, disinflation and a soft landing. A rate rising from 3% to 4% increases by one percentage point, rather than by 1%. Disinflation means a declining inflation rate; deflation means falling prices. A soft landing generally means bringing inflation down without a severe economic downturn. The charts show employment and price developments, not sufficient evidence to declare that a lasting soft landing has occurred. They do not estimate GDP or individual job losses.


Income, purchasing power and growth. Nominal income is income measured in dollars; real purchasing power concerns what it can buy after accounting for prices. Economic growth is an increase in real, or price-adjusted, output. Spending can support business sales, employment and investment, but inflation also depends on supply conditions and other influences. The article discusses these economic channels without estimating wages, consumption, productivity or GDP. It does not infer a household welfare change from unemployment and CPI alone.


Coverage, sources and missing data. Monthly BLS series were acquired through FRED on October 6, 2026. CPI ends in August 2026 and unemployment in September, so joint analysis ends in August. Prices from 2018 supply the 12-month lags for 2019. October 2025 is unavailable in both series; no interpolation is used, and the calendar row remains. See the BLS CPI explanation and CPS explanation. Nearby readings also warrant caution because BLS documents atypical shutdown-related collection and processing. Snapshot values may differ from later revisions.


Research on pandemic inflation. Bernanke, Ben S., and Olivier Blanchard (2023), What Caused the US Pandemic-Era Inflation?, PIIE Working Paper 23-4. Their model emphasizes commodity and sectoral price shocks associated with demand changes and constrained supply in the initial inflation surge, and more persistent pressure from tight labor markets. This external finding does not decompose this article’s full sample or establish that supply alone caused inflation.


Vacancies and disinflation. Crust, Erin E., Kevin J. Lansing, and Nicolas Petrosky-Nadeau (2023), Reducing Inflation along a Nonlinear Phillips Curve, FRBSF Economic Letter 2023-17. Their combined Beveridge-curve and nonlinear Phillips-curve estimates describe a possible adjustment mainly through fewer vacancies, conditional on anchored expectations. Vacancies are unfilled jobs employers are seeking to fill. Their measures are core PCE inflation and unemployment relative to vacancies, unlike this article’s two indicators. The Federal Reserve’s 2% longer-run goal concerns PCE inflation, not CPI.


Policy transmission. Doh, Taeyoung, and Andrew T. Foerster (2022), Have Lags in Monetary Policy Transmission Shortened?, Kansas City Fed Economic Bulletin. Their analysis finds evidence of shorter inflation-response lags after 2009 but substantial uncertainty. It supports caution about timing, not a fixed delay or a forecast for 2026. Additional monitoring priorities and the brief outlook are implications of economic mechanisms and research, not new estimates from this dataset.

title: Why Lower Inflation Does Not Mean Cheaper Living
section: Inflation has eased, but the old prices are gone
text:
Inflation has eased, but the old prices are gone
Inflation describes how quickly prices change. It does not say how much they have changed since a household last found them comfortable. If a price rises from $100 to $108, then rises another 3%, it reaches $111.24. Inflation has fallen from 8% to 3%; the price has risen again.
Figure 1 separates those two measures. The annual inflation rate was 3.4% in August 2026, down from the period’s 9.0% peak in June 2022. Meanwhile, the consumer price index stood at 132.3 on a scale where January 2019 equals 100. That accumulated increase remains part of today’s bills. Lower positive inflation limits further increases; it does not reverse them.








Figure 1: Figure 1. Prices remain elevated even though annual inflation is below its 2022 peak. Separate vertical scales; January 2019 to the latest common month. Source: BLS via FRED. See source note 1.

title: Why Lower Inflation Does Not Mean Cheaper Living
section: The expenses that outran the pay rise
text:
The expenses that outran the pay rise
The national price average also conceals differences among recurring expenses. Since January 2019, grocery prices have risen 33.0%, primary-residence rents 38.1%, and energy prices 57.2%.
Figure 2 compares those increases with the 36.9% rise in average hourly pay. Energy shows the largest increase among the selected categories. Rent has also risen faster than pay; groceries have risen more slowly. These comparisons help explain why an average pay gain may offer less relief to someone whose budget is concentrated in rent and energy.
The bars compare percentage changes, not the dollar cost of one expense with another. A larger energy bar does not establish that energy accounts for the largest part of a family’s spending. Nor can these category increases be added together to explain total inflation. Their practical message is that the composition of a budget matters alongside the national average.








Figure 2: Figure 2. Energy and rent have risen faster than average hourly pay since January 2019. Blue: prices; orange: pay. Changes are percentages, not dollar costs or additive inflation contributions. Source: BLS via FRED. See source note 1.

title: Why Lower Inflation Does Not Mean Cheaper Living
section: A bigger paycheck buys only a little more
text:
A bigger paycheck buys only a little more
To gauge purchasing power, Figure 3 divides the wage increase by the increase in consumer prices. After that adjustment, average real hourly earnings were +3.4% above January 2019 in August 2026. The 36.9% nominal pay rise has therefore translated into a much smaller improvement in what an hour’s earnings can buy.
That is an aggregate result. It does not mean every worker received the average pay rise. The mix of jobs changes over time, so the pandemic-era spike in the chart should not be read as a sudden improvement for all workers. And an hourly wage cannot reveal whether someone has lost paid hours or employment. A household’s actual position also depends on taxes, transfers and its own purchases.








Figure 3: Figure 3. Average real hourly pay is modestly above its January 2019 level. Dashed line: baseline purchasing power. Source: BLS via FRED. See source note 1.

title: Why Lower Inflation Does Not Mean Cheaper Living
section: What would make living more affordable?
text:
What would make living more affordable?
The figures support a limited but useful conclusion: higher prices and a modest gain in average real hourly pay can coexist. They do not establish why prices rose or which policy would bring the greatest relief.
For households comparing a pay offer with living costs, the useful starting point is their own income growth and largest recurring bills over the same period. For policymakers assessing affordability, the implication is to track real earnings and essential expenses alongside the inflation rate, then examine differences across income groups before judging whether relief has reached those under greatest pressure.
The outlook depends on both sides of that comparison. If pay continues to rise faster than prices, purchasing power can improve even without a return to 2019 prices. If it falls behind, low inflation alone will not close the gap. These are conditions to watch, rather than forecasts from these charts.

title: Why Lower Inflation Does Not Mean Cheaper Living
section: Takeaway: Slower inflation is only part of the story
text:
Takeaway: Slower inflation is only part of the story
Consumer prices remain substantially above their 2019 level. Average pay has more than kept pace, but the real gain is modest and says little about any one family’s finances. Affordability improves when income catches up with the bills that people actually pay.

title: The Same House, a Bigger Monthly Bill
text:
A house can stay at the same asking price and still become harder to afford. For a buyer relying on a mortgage, the interest rate changes the monthly commitment attached to that price. A budget that looked comfortable at preapproval can leave less room for the same home when the financing quote changes.
That is the practical question around September’s interest-rate decision: how much does the observed difference in mortgage rates change a buyer’s monthly bill and purchasing budget? The comparison holds the house price, down payment and loan term constant. It measures financing exposure, rather than estimating how the Federal Reserve caused mortgage rates to move.1

title: The Same House, a Bigger Monthly Bill
section: Mortgage rates move on their own timetable
text:
Mortgage rates move on their own timetable
The Federal Reserve raised its target range by a quarter percentage point on September 16, 2026. The weekly 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 6.76% on September 10 and 6.95% on September 17, a change of +19 basis points.
Figure 1 places those observations in context: the selected weeks sit within a longer run of changing financing costs. The September 17 reading largely covers applications received before the announcement, so it cannot be treated as a clean response to the decision. Mortgage pricing reflects longer-term financing conditions and expectations as well as current policy. For a buyer, the relevant number is the available mortgage quote; the weekly average supplies a comparison, not a guaranteed offer.








Figure 1: Figure 1. Weekly mortgage rates around the September 16 meeting (dashed line). Highlighted points: September 10 and 17. Source: Freddie Mac PMMS.

title: The Same House, a Bigger Monthly Bill
section: A small rate difference becomes a recurring bill
text:
A small rate difference becomes a recurring bill
Figure 2 translates rates into monthly payments for three loan sizes. The curves rise with the rate, while a larger loan produces a larger dollar increase for the same rate change. These are fixed-rate, 30-year mortgages. Once the loan is taken out, a later rise in market rates does not automatically raise its scheduled payment.
Consider a home priced at $392,200, with a 20% down payment and a $313,760 loan. This nationally scaled example represents a new-home price benchmark, not a local listing or a typical resale purchase. Under the two September rate scenarios, monthly principal and interest move from $2,037 to $2,077.
The change is +40 dollars a month, or +478 dollars a year. A positive change means a larger bill; a negative one means a smaller bill. Taxes, insurance, fees and maintenance sit on top of these payments. The comparison captures the arithmetic of financing the same principal at different rates; it is not evidence that households actually paid those amounts or kept their loans for 30 years.
