title: The Same House, a Bigger Monthly Bill
section: The same monthly budget supports a different purchase price
text:
The same monthly budget supports a different purchase price
A buyer with a binding monthly limit faces the reverse calculation: how much principal can that payment support? Figure 3 holds the principal-and-interest budget fixed and converts the resulting loan into a home price, assuming a 20% down payment.
At a $2,000 monthly budget, the September 17 scenario supports $377,673, compared with $385,052 a week earlier. At $3,000, the corresponding amounts are $566,510 and $577,578. The percentage change is -1.92% in both cases because supported borrowing is proportional to the payment budget when the rate and term are fixed.
The calculation also assumes the buyer can supply 20% of the resulting price in cash. It does not impose a separate savings limit or represent a lender’s approval decision. A household short of down-payment cash may therefore face a tighter limit than these bars suggest.








Figure 3: Figure 3. Home price supported by the same monthly payment at two mortgage rates. Thirty-year term; down payment equal to 20% of each implied price; other housing costs excluded.

title: The Same House, a Bigger Monthly Bill
section: Budget for the quote, and leave room for uncertainty
text:
Budget for the quote, and leave room for uncertainty
The result is a budgeting warning: affordability depends jointly on price, borrowing and financing cost. Before setting a search price, buyers should reserve room for taxes, insurance and upkeep, then calculate how much of the remaining monthly budget can service the loan. Comparing lender quotes also requires comparing points and fees, which these scenarios exclude.
An illustrative stress test shows the value of leaving room. With a $2,500 monthly principal-and-interest budget, rates 50 or 100 basis points above the September 17 average reduce the supported price by a further $22,964 or $44,175, respectively. These are scenarios, not forecasts or universal lending thresholds.
If rates fall, buying power can improve at an unchanged price; if they rise, the same budget supports less borrowing. Future refinancing is an option to evaluate, not a reliable way to rescue an unaffordable purchase today.

The September comparison changes monthly principal and interest by +40 dollars for the benchmark loan, and supported purchase price by -1.92% at a fixed payment budget. A sustainable purchase begins with an all-in monthly limit, a realistic down payment and a financing quote that leaves room for uncertainty.

title: When Young Children Are at Home, Who Is at Work?
text:
When a young child needs care, a household must find time, pay for help or combine the two. That decision can shape earnings, staffing and access to paid work. Yet talking about “parents’ employment” as a single outcome risks hiding how differently care and work fit together for women and men.
How does employment differ between adults with a young child at home and those without a minor child at home—and does the comparison point in the same direction for women and men? Among Americans aged 25–54 in 2025, the comparison shows lower employment for women and higher employment for men. The analysis below separates participation from unemployment and asks whether broad age and education adjustments change that picture.1

title: When Young Children Are at Home, Who Is at Work?
section: Young children and employment: compare women and men separately
text:
Young children and employment: compare women and men separately
Among women whose youngest own child at home is aged 0–5, 67.7% are employed, compared with 77.5% among women with no own minor child at home. That is a difference of -9.9 percentage points. For men, the corresponding rates are 93.6% and 80.9%: a difference of +12.7 percentage points for the young-child group.
Figure 1 also shows the comparison for older children. It is a picture of different households at one point in time, rather than a family’s path as a child grows up. “No minor child at home” does not mean never having children: it includes adults with grown children or children living elsewhere.








Figure 1: Figure 1. Employment rates by recorded sex and youngest own child at home, ages 25–54. Weighted 2025 IPUMS CPS ASEC estimates; source note explains the comparison.

title: When Young Children Are at Home, Who Is at Work?
section: Participation and unemployment tell different parts of the story
text:
Participation and unemployment tell different parts of the story
A lower employment rate can mean fewer people are in the labor force, more participants are unemployed, or both. Figure 2 separates employed adults, unemployed adults and adults outside the labor force, so each group’s bar accounts for everyone.
Among women in the young-child group, 69.8% participate in the labor force, compared with 80.3% in the reference group. Their unemployment rates are 3.0% and 3.5%, respectively. The participation component is larger in absolute size than the unemployment component. An accounting decomposition assigns -10.2 percentage points to the participation margin and +0.3 percentage points to the unemployment margin. Together they reproduce the employment difference; they do not identify its causes.
That distinction matters for policy. Help with finding a job addresses a different obstacle from help making paid work compatible with care. The chart does not establish why people are outside the labor force, however; it cannot separate care responsibilities, health, preferences or other constraints.








Figure 2: Figure 2. Employment, unemployment and nonparticipation as shares of all adults. The unemployed segment is not the unemployment rate. Weighted 2025 IPUMS CPS ASEC estimates.

title: When Young Children Are at Home, Who Is at Work?
section: After age and education adjustment: what the model and Figure 3 show
text:
After age and education adjustment: what the model and Figure 3 show
Adults with young children differ from the comparison group in more than household composition. A weighted linear probability model checks whether the pattern remains after accounting for age bands and whether someone has a bachelor’s degree. Employment is coded one for an employed adult and zero otherwise. The model allows the youngest-child association to differ between women and men:
\[
E_i=\alpha+\beta F_i+\sum_g\gamma_g C_{ig}
+\sum_g\delta_g(F_i C_{ig})+\boldsymbol{\theta}'A_i+\lambda B_i+u_i.
\]
Here \(F_i\) identifies women, \(C_{ig}\) the child-age groups, \(A_i\) age bands and \(B_i\) degree status. Relative to no minor child at home, the young-child difference is \(\gamma_{\text{young}}\) for men and \(\gamma_{\text{young}}+\delta_{\text{young}}\) for women. Multiplying by 100 gives percentage points. The table reports those two contrasts and their difference; Figure 3 plots the first two, with 95% confidence intervals.

The adjusted differences are -10.7 percentage points for women and +11.2 percentage points for men. Their contrast is -21.9 percentage points. The women’s interval is below zero; the men’s interval is above zero. The interaction interval is below zero. An interval crossing zero signals uncertainty about the direction of that contrast. The model sharpens the description; it does not show what having a child would do to any particular person’s employment. Partner earnings, care availability, preferences and selection into parenthood remain outside this adjustment.

title: When Young Children Are at Home, Who Is at Work?
section: Supporting work requires looking beyond unemployment
text:
Supporting work requires looking beyond unemployment
The comparison associates young children at home with lower employment for women and higher employment for men. The participation component is larger in absolute size than the unemployment component. Employers considering retention should examine predictable schedules, flexibility and barriers to returning after leave. Policymakers assessing childcare support should measure access to paid work as well as unemployment, and evaluate whether support reaches households facing the strongest constraints.
These are directions for investigation, not proven remedies from this comparison. Establishing which intervention works requires evidence on care costs and availability, household circumstances, and changes over time. If support enables adults who want paid work to participate, employment may increase even without a large change in the unemployment rate.

title: When Young Children Are at Home, Who Is at Work?
section: Takeaway: One “parent employment” figure misses the divide
text:
Takeaway: One “parent employment” figure misses the divide
At the same ages, the raw young-child employment differences are -9.9 percentage points for women and +12.7 percentage points for men; after broad age and education adjustment they are -10.7 percentage points and +11.2 percentage points. The findings identify where to look—participation and the conditions for combining care with work—while leaving the causes and effective remedies to further research.

title: Did Cooler Inflation Have to Cost Americans Their Jobs?
section: From lost paychecks to rising bills
text:
From lost paychecks to rising bills
The prices households pay for goods and services, including groceries, rent and transport, are consumer prices. The Consumer Price Index (CPI) tracks the cost of a representative basket, with more weight given to items households spend more on. Inflation measures its rate of increase; here, the year-on-year rate compares a month with the same month one year earlier. It describes an average basket, not every family’s bill.
The labor force consists of employed people and people classified as unemployed. The unemployment rate is the unemployed share of that group. People generally must be without work, available for work and have actively searched in the previous four weeks; those awaiting recall from temporary layoff can qualify without searching. Retirees and people neither working nor seeking work are generally outside the labor force. A low unemployment rate therefore does not mean everyone has a job.2
Figure 1 shows that the two crises arrived at different times. Unemployment rose from 3.5% in February 2020 to 14.8% in April. Annual inflation fell to 0.3%. By June 2022, inflation reached 9.1%, while unemployment stood at 3.6%.
For households, the first shock threatened earnings and the ability to pay bills. Lost income and fear of unemployment can reduce spending, especially on discretionary purchases. Weaker sales can then discourage firms from hiring and investing, putting further pressure on employment and economic growth, the expansion of price-adjusted output. These are economic channels, not effects measured by Figure 1.
As unemployment receded, more people could earn and spend again. But faster price increases squeezed what a paycheck could buy unless income kept pace. Lower unemployment can therefore coexist with financial strain. The figure shows this change in pressures; it does not establish that recovering employment caused inflation.
Looking ahead, continued employment can support consumption and growth if incomes keep pace with prices. Slower hiring or renewed inflation would threaten that balance. These are conditional implications: Figure 1 does not measure job openings, future job-finding chances or output growth.


Figure 1Unemployment surged first; inflation followed as jobs recovered


Question answered: How did the two pressures evolve over time? Finding: The unemployment shock preceded the inflation peak, shifting the household concern from lost earnings toward rising bills.

How to read the rates and household implications


The panels share the calendar and a 0-16% vertical scale. Inflation is a change in the price index; unemployment is a labor-force share. A falling inflation rate can still mean prices are rising. A falling unemployment rate can reflect more employment, people leaving the labor force, or both. Consequently, this chart cannot by itself measure household welfare or hiring prospects. Inflation uses unadjusted CPI over 12 months; unemployment is seasonally adjusted. The gray band is missing data, not a collapse in either rate. The endpoint labels refer to the latest common month.

title: Did Cooler Inflation Have to Cost Americans Their Jobs?
section: Why one fixed Phillips-curve trade-off does not fit these months
text:
Why one fixed Phillips-curve trade-off does not fit these months
When employers compete for scarce workers, pay can rise and firms may pass some costs into prices. The Phillips curve describes the proposed short-run relationship between inflation and spare capacity in the labor market. Its familiar downward-sloping version associates lower unemployment with higher inflation, holding other influences constant. It is not a permanent menu of policy choices.
Figure 2 places each month’s unemployment rate on the horizontal axis and inflation on the vertical axis, bringing that relationship into view. It shows that similar unemployment rates accompanied very different inflation rates, so one fixed curve cannot summarize this episode. This does not invalidate Phillips-curve models that allow expectations, supply conditions and labor-market tightness to change.
Figure 2 shows why that qualification matters. In February 2020, unemployment was 3.5% and inflation 2.3%. In June 2022, almost the same unemployment rate accompanied inflation near 9.1%. A similar jobs market therefore coincided with sharply different pressure on household budgets.
Why might the relationship change? Bernanke and Blanchard’s pandemic-inflation study emphasizes commodity-price increases and shifts in demand against constrained supply, while finding more persistent pressures from tight labor markets. Their model supplies an explanation that this scatterplot cannot identify on its own.6 The implication for households and policymakers is that the unemployment rate alone cannot explain the pace of price increases.


Figure 2Similar unemployment, different inflation: no single fixed trade-off


Connection to the Phillips curve: This chart compares inflation with unemployment directly. Finding: Similar unemployment rates coincide with different inflation pressures, showing why other influences matter.



Blue: Jan 2019-Feb 2020Orange: Mar 2020-Jun 2022Green: Jul 2022-Dec 2024Purple: Jan 2025 onward


Source: Author’s calculations using BLS data via FRED. January 2019 to August 2026. Definitions and source notes.



How this chart relates to the Phillips curve


Each colored dot is one month with both rates available. Moving right means more unemployment; moving up means faster annual price increases. A textbook downward-sloping curve would describe a conditional relationship: less inflation when unemployment is higher, with other factors held constant. These observed months do not hold those factors constant. Inflation expectations are beliefs about future price increases; supply shocks change production costs or availability; labor-market tightness concerns how difficult it is for employers to find workers. All can influence the inflation-unemployment relationship. The thin gray line connects months chronologically, breaking across October 2025. It is not a fitted regression or an estimate of a structural curve. The chart neither identifies a causal effect nor disproves a conditional Phillips curve. White circles identify the checkpoints in Figure 3; colors organize descriptive periods.

title: Did Cooler Inflation Have to Cost Americans Their Jobs?
section: Did the inflation retreat require a large increase in unemployment?
text:
Did the inflation retreat require a large increase in unemployment?
Between June 2022 and December 2024, inflation fell by 6.2 percentage points, while unemployment rose by 0.5 points. A percentage point is the difference between two rates: moving from 3% to 4% is one point, not a 1% increase.
Figure 3 compares changes between selected monthly endpoints, making the jobs side of the inflation retreat explicit. Falling inflation, or disinflation, coincided with a modest unemployment increase through 2024. That is consistent with one aspect of a soft landing: lowering inflation without a severe downturn. It does not prove that monetary policy caused the decline or that every household benefited; a small national increase can still conceal serious losses for particular workers.
The latest period also complicates the story. By August 2026, inflation was 3.4%, above December 2024’s 2.9%, while unemployment was 4.1%, unchanged between those endpoints. The improvement was substantial, but the inflation problem did not simply disappear.


Figure 3A large inflation decline coincided with a small unemployment rise


Question answered: Did the post-peak decline accompany a large unemployment increase? Finding: From June 2022 to December 2024, inflation fell 6.2 points while unemployment rose 0.5 points.

How to read this chart


Each bar subtracts the starting month’s rate from the ending month’s rate. These are percentage-point changes, not cumulative price increases, monthly growth rates, period averages or policy effects. The periods have different lengths and are chosen to highlight the pandemic shock, reopening, the inflation peak and subsequent developments. Endpoint comparisons do not capture every movement within a period. The final unemployment bar is zero; that does not imply an unchanged labor market throughout the interval.

title: Did Cooler Inflation Have to Cost Americans Their Jobs?
section: A softer landing depends on how the economy adjusts
text:
A softer landing depends on how the economy adjusts
Together, the figures establish the sequence, show why a fixed trade-off is inadequate, and quantify the post-peak comparison. They support a narrow conclusion: substantial disinflation occurred alongside a modest unemployment increase through 2024. They cannot allocate credit among monetary policy, changing supply conditions and shifts in demand.
External research suggests one possible route. Crust, Lansing and Petrosky-Nadeau find that cooling can occur mainly through fewer job vacancies, meaning unfilled positions employers are seeking to fill, rather than much higher unemployment. Their model’s soft-landing path also depends on stable long-run inflation expectations.7 That distinction matters: fewer advertised openings can make a job search harder even when existing workers largely keep their jobs. Vacancies are not measured in this post.
The policy implication is to watch hiring, vacancies, labor-force participation, inflation expectations and wage growth relative to productivity alongside the headline rates. Weak hiring can signal emerging risks; an unemployment increase caused by more people entering the labor force has a different interpretation from one driven by layoffs. Monetary policy also works with uncertain delays, so waiting for either inflation or unemployment alone to settle may miss developing pressures.8 These are monitoring priorities, not an estimated prescription for interest rates.
The outlook depends on the source of adjustment. If supply improves and hiring remains resilient, price pressures can ease while consumption and output expand. If restraint instead weakens spending and firms cut recruitment, slower growth and greater job insecurity become risks. Renewed supply disruptions could raise prices without stronger demand. These are scenarios informed by economic mechanisms and research, not forecasts generated by the two series.

title: Did Cooler Inflation Have to Cost Americans Their Jobs?
section: Takeaway: Lower inflation need not mean a jobs crisis
text:
Takeaway: Lower inflation need not mean a jobs crisis
The pandemic first disrupted work, then brought an inflation surge during the recovery. Similar unemployment rates accompanied different inflation pressures; after the 2022 peak, inflation fell sharply with only a modest unemployment increase through 2024. The latest endpoint comparison nevertheless shows renewed inflation pressure, so lasting relief cannot be assumed. Research helps explain how supply adjustment and vacancy reductions might limit employment losses, but this post does not estimate those mechanisms. The conclusion is to judge progress by prices, job access and purchasing power together. Lower inflation can protect living standards when earnings and employment hold up; a better headline rate alone cannot establish that households are better off.

The retreat from the inflation peak was markedly different from the pandemic collapse. Between June 2022 and December 2024, inflation fell from 9.1% to 2.9%, while unemployment rose from 3.6% to 4.1%.
That combination supports part of the case for a soft landing: substantial disinflation accompanied relatively limited deterioration in the labor market.4 It does not establish the contribution of interest rates, or erase the losses borne by workers who became unemployed.


Figure 3. Inflation’s retreat brought a modest rise in unemployment


From June 2022 to December 2024, inflation fell 6.2 points while unemployment rose 0.5 points.

Source: BLS via FRED; author’s calculations. Changes in percentage points between named months.



Chart notes


Each bar subtracts the starting rate from the ending rate. The intervals differ in length. Bars represent endpoint differences, not period averages, cumulative price increases or estimated policy effects. A zero unemployment change between endpoints does not imply no movement within the interval.



The improvement did not continue at the same pace. By August 2026, inflation was 3.4%, above its December 2024 reading, while unemployment remained at 4.1%. Stable unemployment between those dates did not imply an uninterrupted decline in price pressures.
The next adjustment will depend partly on how the labor market cools. Research by Crust, Lansing and Petrosky-Nadeau describes a possible path through fewer vacancies rather than sharply higher unemployment, provided inflation expectations remain stable.8 Even then, fewer openings can make finding work harder.
Policymakers should watch hiring, vacancies, participation and wage growth relative to productivity alongside inflation. Uncertain policy delays strengthen the case for weighing several indicators together.9 Further relief would require easing price pressures while employment and purchasing power hold up; renewed supply disruptions or weaker demand could make that balance harder to sustain.

title: When Young Children Are at Home, Who Is at Work?
text:
Among women in the young-child group, 67.7% are employed, against 77.5% among women with no own minor child at home. The equivalent figures for men are 93.6% and 80.9%. These percentages count adults with a job out of all adults in each group.3
Figure 1 sets that comparison beside households with older children. A rate of 80% means about 80 adults in work per 100 in the group. A gap of ten percentage points means a difference of ten employed adults per 100, rather than a ten per cent relative change.4
For households, access to paid work can affect the ability to earn or withstand a lost wage. But the chart does not measure pay, hours or financial hardship. It also cannot show how a particular family’s employment changed after a birth: each bar describes different people at one point in time.

text:
Having no job is not always counted as unemployment. The labor force includes adults who are employed and those who are unemployed; people neither working nor meeting the unemployment definition are outside it. This distinction separates participation in paid work from success in finding it.3
Women living with a young child have a participation rate of 69.8%, compared with 80.3% in the reference group. Among participants, unemployment is 3.0% and 3.5%, respectively.


Figure 2. Having no job is not always unemployment


Each bar divides all adults in its group between work, job search and nonparticipation.

Chart notes


The segments sum to 100% of all adults. The unemployed segment is not the unemployment rate, whose denominator is labor-force participants. Outside the labor force does not identify childcare as the reason for nonparticipation. Men and women use the same scale.



An accounting breakdown assigns -10.2 percentage points of the women’s employment gap to participation differences and +0.3 percentage points to unemployment differences. The participation component is larger in absolute size than the unemployment component. The two components add to the observed employment gap; they do not identify what caused it.5
For employers and policymakers, that distinction changes the question. A participation gap prompts examination of whether paid work can fit household circumstances. An unemployment gap concerns job finding among those already in the labor force. The bars cannot distinguish care responsibilities from health, preferences or other reasons for not participating.

title: When Young Children Are at Home, Who Is at Work?
text:
Adults living with young children may differ in age and qualifications from the reference group. A weighted linear probability model compares their employment while allowing for three age bands and whether they hold a bachelor’s degree. It also allows the child-group association to differ for women and men.6
For women, adjustment changes the gap from -9.9 percentage points to -10.7 percentage points. For men, it changes from +12.7 percentage points to +11.2 percentage points. Both associations retain their direction: broad age and education differences do not explain away the pattern.

Positive bars indicate higher employment in the young-child group, negative bars lower employment. Both panels use the same signed scale and zero line. Adjusted 95% confidence intervals appear in the table below. Adjustment is a conditional association, not the effect of having a child.



The model’s outcome is one when an adult is employed and zero otherwise. Its coefficients therefore describe differences in the probability of employment; multiplying a contrast by 100 expresses it in percentage points. The specification is:

\[
E_i=\alpha+\beta F_i+\sum_g\gamma_g C_{ig}
+\sum_g\delta_g(F_i C_{ig})+\boldsymbol{\theta}'A_i+\lambda B_i+u_i.
\]

Here \(F_i\) identifies women, \(C_{ig}\) child-age groups, \(A_i\) age bands and \(B_i\) degree status. The no-minor-child group is the reference. The young-child contrast is \(\gamma_{\text{young}}\) for men and \(\gamma_{\text{young}}+\delta_{\text{young}}\) for women. Adjustment makes the comparison more specific, but it leaves partner earnings, care availability and selection into parenthood unaccounted for. The model describes an employment association among broadly comparable adults. It does not estimate what having a child would do to an individual’s job prospects.

title: When Young Children Are at Home, Who Is at Work?
text:
The participation breakdown and adjusted comparison locate the employment difference more precisely than a single parenthood average. They do not establish which constraint caused it or how much a particular policy would change it.
Employers examining retention can assess whether schedules, leave and return-to-work arrangements fit the needs of staff with care responsibilities. Policymakers evaluating childcare provision should examine participation alongside unemployment and test whether support reaches adults who want paid work. These are priorities for assessment, rather than remedies whose effects this model has measured.
If more reliable care and workable schedules enable additional adults to participate, employment could rise without a large fall in unemployment. Testing that possibility requires evidence over time and a credible evaluation. This cross-section cannot forecast employment or household income.

title: When Young Children Are at Home, Who Is at Work?
text:
Population, sources and coverage. Author’s analysis of the 2025 IPUMS CPS ASEC, sample cps2025_03s, ages 25–54 with valid analysis variables and positive ASECWT. This is a single cross-section, not a truncated 2024–2026 series. Downloaded person records include ages and cases outside the analytic sample; sample_audit.csv documents selection. CPS is a household survey; ASEC is its annual social and economic supplement.
 Children and recorded sex. YNGCH describes the youngest own biological, adopted or stepchild at home. “No minor child” includes no own child present or a youngest own child aged 18 or older. It does not identify adults who have never been parents. Recorded sex is not a measure of gender identity.
 Employment, participation and unemployment. Employment divides employed adults by all adults in the group. Participation divides employed plus unemployed adults by all adults. Unemployment divides unemployed adults by labor-force participants; the classification includes people on temporary layoff under the applicable definition. Figure 2 instead divides every status by all adults.
 Percentage points and household implications. 80% minus 70% is ten percentage points, not a ten per cent relative increase. A group employment-rate difference is not a count of individuals who left work after childbirth. Household-income, hours and care mechanisms discussed in the article are interpretations to investigate, not additional estimates from these figures.
 Participation breakdown. Employment equals participation multiplied by one minus unemployment. With \(L\) for participation, \(U\) for unemployment, \(y\) for young-child households and \(n\) for the reference, the employment gap is \(100(L_y-L_n)(1-U_n)-100L_y(U_y-U_n)\). The two components use the reference unemployment rate and the young-child participation rate. This accounting identity is not a causal decomposition.
 Model and comparisons. The specification is employed ~ sex * child_group + age_band + college. References are men, no minor child, ages 25–34 and below bachelor’s degree. Age bands are 25–34, 35–44 and 45–54. The linear model can produce fitted probabilities outside zero and one; model diagnostics record that limitation. Adjusted bars are coefficient contrasts at common controls, not observed employment rates.
 Weights and uncertainty. ASECWT supplies person weights. Uncertainty uses all 160 REPWTP person replicate weights, successive-difference replication and mse=TRUE. Contrasts use t(159) intervals and account for covariance between main and interaction terms. See IPUMS replicate-weight guidance. Observed gaps have no intervals in this table; the displayed intervals refer to adjusted contrasts. Full parameters and diagnostics are exported on a microdata run.
 Execution and publication status. Execution mode: original microdata re-estimated in this run. A reference preview permits inspection of the draft. A new raw-data run and editorial review are required before final publication.
